title: 5 Questions That Could Reshape AI
dek: Anthropic prices the most consequential AI IPO yet while the Jensen Huang saga reverberates from Wall Street to the Situation Room. Five questions will shape this week: how the IPO goes, whether OpenAI or a Chinese lab tries to steal the spotlight, whether Jensen comes back, whether Howard Lutnick takes the fall, and whether Congress finally moves on export controls.

oneIdea.headline: This is a before-and-after week for AI, and Anthropic's IPO is the hinge.
oneIdea.summary: Anthropic's IPO was always going to be a landmark. Add last week's Jensen Huang scandal and it becomes a moment the history books will mark. For years, investors have used Nvidia, the neoclouds and stock-market machinations as bad proxies for the only question that matters: will AI demand justify the cost? Once Anthropic is public, every quarter brings fresh evidence for that debate. Around it swirl four more questions that will shape far more than AI: OpenAI's next move, Jensen's possible return, Lutnick's exposure and the fate of export controls.

gpCorner.note: AI commentary for UK general practice; not from the podcast

items.title: A public Anthropic means published accounts
items.body: Several NHS scribe and triage tools run on Anthropic's models. Once it is listed, it must publish audited figures every quarter. NLW welcomes that as real evidence of demand; Zitron expects it to show a company spending far ahead of income. Either way it is useful to us: for the first time a buyer can read the finances of the firm underneath its supplier.

items.title: Treat the cure-for-cancer pitch as a pitch
items.body: Anthropic's chief executive told investors he hopes heart disease, Alzheimer's and cancer become relics like smallpox. That was said on a roadshow, selling shares. It is a hope, not a result, and nothing in it changes what we offer patients. NLW reports it without much challenge; Zitron did not address it.

items.title: Supplier resilience
items.body: Zitron's account is that Nvidia's money kept many smaller AI firms alive and that this has now stopped. NLW also expects credit to tighten. If either is right, some health technology start-ups will find funding harder next year. Before renewing, ask a supplier how long its cash lasts and what happens to the service and the data if it is sold or closes.

the_other_side.text: Zitron, writing a day later, argues there is no independent AI demand for the Anthropic flotation to reveal. In his account the appetite for chips and computing was manufactured by Nvidia, which funded its own customers, guaranteed their leases and pressed buyers to take chips early; he notes it joined 129 venture deals this year, 27 per cent of global deal value. He says Anthropic will not be cash-flow positive before 2030, carries $895 billion in compute commitments, and that its growth is slowing to 15 to 25 per cent a quarter. He insists Huang "resigned and is not coming back", and that the financing he ran has ended.

the_truth_beneath.text: The variable both men orbit is whether demand for AI exists apart from the money Nvidia and investors pushed into it. Both accept as fact that Nvidia backstopped labs and cloud firms, that Anthropic has roughly $900 billion of compute commitments with about $70 billion due within a year, and that its flotation matters. The empirical question is whether Anthropic's revenue keeps growing once that support recedes; the observable is its first quarterly reports as a public company, beginning with fourth-quarter growth against the 15 to 25 per cent Ramp expects. The residue is worldview: whether a business that must spend ahead of revenue is investing or merely surviving. For Whittemore to be vindicated, public filings must show customer demand growing fast enough to carry the commitments. For Zitron, growth must slow as venture-funded customers run short and financing tightens. Both are polemicists with incentives: Whittemore bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype. The signal is that both say Nvidia was a poor guide to real demand. Watch Anthropic's first earnings report.

headlines.headline: Anthropic is about to become the world's most important AI stock
headlines.summary: Bloomberg's headline captures the stakes. Expectations for markets, the American economy and even geopolitics are bundled into this one IPO. First trading is slated for Thursday the 19th, with final pricing the day before.

headlines.headline: From $2 trillion dreams to a $1.4 trillion target, and bankers pushing back up
headlines.summary: Peak-bullish investors once talked about a $2T valuation. As the AI trade soured, the target fell to $1.25–1.4T, which some banking partners reportedly plan to push to $1.5T. The raise is $57–64B from IPO buyers plus $26B in private placement led by Nvidia and Google, more than $90B all in. Anthropic reportedly cares more about cash raised than about the perfect valuation.

headlines.headline: Demand is running nearly seven times supply
headlines.summary: The deal was reportedly six times oversubscribed last Thursday and closing on seven by the weekend. One source called demand hotter than SpaceX at this stage and compared it to Snowflake's 2020 IPO, which popped 112% on day one. The difference is scale: Anthropic is raising three times Snowflake's entire valuation at the time.

headlines.headline: The cynical case: Anthropic can't afford a broken IPO
headlines.summary: Scott Galloway argues that whatever the fundamentals, the first trade is almost certain to rip. He expects it 15–40% above pricing because Anthropic would rather take more dilution than face a 'broken IPO' headline. His risk-adjusted play is to get an allocation and sell on the first trade.

headlines.headline: Compute is the deepest business dilemma that the company faces.
headlines.attribution: Dario Amodei, Anthropic CEO, at the company's investor day
headlines.summary: At a JPMorgan investor day hosted by Jamie Dimon, Amodei said the field is moving so fast technologically that nobody knows how it will translate into economic value, which leaves Anthropic with 'huge uncertainty.' Wall Street is struggling to value a company that fits no standard tech profile.

headlines.headline: Anthropic is deliberately overbuying compute, and $71B comes due this year
headlines.summary: Anthropic has disclosed more than $900B in compute commitments over the decade, with $71B due in the next year. Amodei said an earlier bet on too little compute cost the company customers and R&D cycles and stunted revenue growth. Buying too much carries its own risk: financial overextension.

headlines.headline: Nvidia was always a terrible proxy for the real question
headlines.summary: Analysts call Anthropic the new bellwether, maybe more important than Nvidia now that Jensen is gone. NLW goes further. Even with Jensen still there, everything investors watched failed to answer the only question that matters: will AI demand justify the cost? Once Anthropic is public, every quarter brings real evidence for that debate.

headlines.headline: The overlooked story: Anthropic is shipping whole apps at a blistering pace
headlines.summary: Last week alone brought a productivity suite and then a video-meetings app. Just as Opus 4.5 let Claude Code ship features almost daily, internal models may now be letting Anthropic ship entire products. It is chipping away at nearly every major software category.

headlines.headline: David Sacks accuses Anthropic of building the world's most valuable monopoly
headlines.summary: The former AI czar says Anthropic's 'winner-take-all' roadshow language describes a monopoly. He also charges that the company calls recursive self-improvement the most dangerous work there is while marketing it to investors as a business advantage.

headlines.headline: The roadshow pitch: end disease, then everything else
headlines.summary: Amodei told investors he hopes heart disease, Alzheimer's and cancer become relics like smallpox: 'It sounds crazy. I really do believe it.' One account of a pre-IPO broker call went further. It described a pitch about taking on hyperscalers, every other lab, biotech and robotics, with a $1T ARR target by Q4 2028.

headlines.headline: Will OpenAI try to steal Anthropic's IPO spotlight?
headlines.summary: With the IPO now looking safe, and Amodei taking potshots ('We don't vague post about models ahead of time'), OpenAI has reason to ship. Leaker Token Gremlin showed outputs said to come from a GPT-6.2 Astra preview. They also reported that API resellers already have the model, which, if true, means a release is close.

headlines.headline: Chinese models don't need to be good to spook Wall Street
headlines.summary: A Chinese release only has to look strong long enough to drive a narrative cycle. Moonshot and DeepSeek look unlikely right now. Qwen 4 Max claims benchmark wins over Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1, but real-world tests look lackluster. One developer's diagnosis: since Anthropic shut the door on distillation, Chinese models 'haven't moved an inch.'

headlines.headline: OpenAI's frontier-model drought hits 72 days
headlines.summary: That is the longest gap since GPT-5 to 5.1. A few more weeks without a release would make it the longest since o3 to GPT-5. Whether or not a model lands this week, something has to come soon.

headlines.headline: Is OpenAI in third place? Not quite consensus, but bubbling
headlines.summary: A growing narrative says OpenAI has fallen behind. NLW agrees that Opus 5.5 is ahead. He thinks Google, despite a strong Gemini 4 Carbon, still has more to prove before it can claim second.

headlines.headline: A possible reason for the delay: Washington now gates model launches
headlines.summary: OpenAI's Rune says people underestimate federal involvement: a new model must be shown to be safe to the government before launch, or export-control bans follow. NLW's bet is a new OpenAI model soon after the Anthropic IPO, with Thanksgiving complicating the timing.

headlines.headline: The Bring Back Jensen movement crosses 175,000 signatures
headlines.summary: A new open letter counts more than 10,000 current and former Nvidia employees and 90,000 shareholders among its signers. The effort reportedly has Jensen's support. Shareholders Gavin Baker and Brad Gerstner also wrote to the board urging a deliberate process that keeps his return on the table.

headlines.headline: 'Resigned,' not fired, gives the board a way back
headlines.summary: The New York Times reports that Trump urged Jensen to fight for his job, seeing the economy as tied to his personal leadership. Gene Munster raised his odds of a return to 51% from 10%, while Kalshi sits at 9%. Because Jensen technically resigned, the board can welcome him back without admitting it fired him. Balaji Srinivasan argues it is a fait accompli if Jensen simply asks.

headlines.headline: The mainstream sees a sex scandal; the real story is the chips
headlines.summary: SNL framed the saga as a midlife crisis that tanked markets, plus a skit about the CIA teaching billionaires to spot spies. NLW points out what all of it misses: the security implications of Jensen potentially knowing that chips were reaching China.

headlines.headline: The spy angle is getting murkier
headlines.summary: DealBook accused David Sacks of spreading conspiracy theories, but he was amplifying CNN reporting that CIA and DOJ officials aren't certain Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. Taylor Lorenz defended him. Adding another curveball, Megaspeed says she left the firm in August of last year.

headlines.headline: It doesn't matter to me whether she's a spy or not.
headlines.attribution: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, on the Sunday shows
headlines.summary: Bessent wants the board to look outside the company for a 'dramatic shakeup.' He calls the real question whether Nvidia's culture pushed seemingly illicit sales to pass-through shell companies to goose revenue. He wants answers from the board and outside counsel within 10 days.

headlines.headline: SemiAnalysis: 1.5GW of Nvidia chips are in China illegally
headlines.summary: Dylan Patel argues Nvidia definitely knew. He says unwinding the web of how those chips got there is what makes this dangerous, and why the board moved so fast. Whether the board acted to stave off investor lawsuits or because intelligence agencies came asking determines whether Jensen's return is even in its hands.

headlines.headline: Tuesday's earnings won't be the story; the China questions will
headlines.summary: Nvidia has beaten estimates 15 quarters in a row and likely will again. Interim CEO Colette Kress should expect early questions about chips going to China. Dan Ives sees 'no chance' Jensen returns, arguing the rockstar persona is gone for good.

headlines.headline: Lutnick emerges as the scandal's central Washington figure
headlines.summary: Lutnick reportedly stalled three times on cracking down on Megaspeed. The NYT says Nvidia's general counsel inserted comments directly into Commerce policy drafts. He testifies before Senate Banking on December 10. Bessent says only that 'Commerce has the pen,' and some Democrats say the scandal goes all the way to the president.

headlines.headline: With Jensen gone, who's left to lobby against export controls?
headlines.summary: Three export-control bills, including one closing the remote-access loophole for Southeast Asian data centers, are headed into must-pass NDAA negotiations. Speaker Mike Johnson sees a 'developing consensus.' With both OpenAI and Anthropic backing tougher controls, the status quo has almost no defenders left.
